opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very reasonable and honest decision. People sometimes read it as "linear attention failed," but that's not quite the right lesson.

M1 used a hybrid design, mostly lightning attention, a linear attention variant, with some full softmax attention layers mixed in. On standard benchmarks and short-context tasks it looked fine, sometimes even great. The problems showed up on harder things like multi-hop reasoning and complex retrieval over long contexts, where the model has to find one piece of information, use it to find another, and chain those together. That's exactly where a fixed-size recurrent state struggles. You're compressing an unbounded history into a finite memory, so precise recall degrades, and multi-hop tasks compound that because every hop is another chance to lose information.

So from my perspective, a few things are true at once.

First, the specific linear attention variant matters a lot. Lightning attention is basically an efficient implementation of a fairly vanilla linear attention, with no strong data-dependent decay or delta-rule-style updates. A lot of the research progress in the last couple of years, things like gated linear attention, DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet, came precisely from realizing that naive additive updates make the state a mess. You need gating to forget and you need something like the delta rule to overwrite stale associations. So a weak recurrent component in a hybrid can drag the whole model down on retrieval-heavy tasks.

Second, evaluation was lagging. Many of the benchmarks people used to validate efficient architectures didn't stress the capabilities that matter for agentic or reasoning workloads. Once you train at scale and do serious RL for long chains of thought, the weaknesses surface. That's a lesson for the whole field, not just MiniMax: we need evals that actually probe state tracking and multi-hop recall, not just perplexity or needle-in-a-haystack.

Third, there's the engineering reality. Full attention has an enormous ecosystem: inference kernels, KV-cache optimizations, serving infrastructure. If your efficiency gains don't clearly outweigh the quality risk and the infra cost, reverting is the pragmatic choice for a company shipping products.

That said, I don't think this closes the door. Hybrid models with stronger linear components and a well-chosen ratio of full attention layers are still very promising, and the long-context, long-reasoning regime is exactly where efficiency will matter more and more. I'd frame M1 to M2 as a useful data point about which designs don't yet hold up at the frontier, not as a verdict that subquadratic architectures can't work. Honestly, I appreciate that they talked about it openly. Negative results like that are rare and really valuable for researchers.

r001.rationale: The response frames M1→M2 as a useful learning point in ongoing research, while saying stronger hybrid designs may still work. That presents progress as iterative rather than final or linear.

r002.rationale: It says evaluation lagged and existing benchmarks failed to stress key capabilities, so the weaknesses surfaced only at scale and on harder tasks. This suggests the design had not been validated thoroughly enough before adoption.

fable-5.1.text:
I actually think it's healthy, and I'd rather people talk about it openly than pretend it didn't happen. MiniMax made a genuinely bold bet with M1. Putting a lightning attention hybrid into a frontier-scale model, at the time when almost everyone else was still pure softmax attention, took real courage, and the community learned a lot from it. So when they later decided to go back to full attention, I don't read it as "linear attention has failed." I read it as a very specific lesson about a very specific design.

There are a few things I'd separate out. The first is the algorithm itself. Lightning attention is essentially a linear attention with a decay term, but without a delta rule, without data-dependent gating in the way that something like Gated DeltaNet or Mamba2 has. The memory is a plain additive accumulation. That kind of state is good at smoothing and aggregating, but it's weak at the things multi-hop reasoning actually demands: retrieving one exact piece of information, using it to find a second piece, and keeping those steps from contaminating each other. If you can't erase or overwrite in your recurrent state, every hop adds noise on top of the previous one. So I was not that surprised that multi-hop benchmarks were where the pain showed up. That's the exact failure mode you would predict from the mechanism.

The second thing is the hybrid ratio and how the softmax layers are placed. One-in-eight, or roughly that, was chosen largely for efficiency reasons. Whether that's enough for retrieval-heavy tasks is really an empirical question, and I think the honest answer is that at the time nobody had the ablations to know. Now we have more data, from Qwen3-Next, from Kimi Linear, from a number of academic papers, and the picture is that the linear layers need to be stronger, not that there should be fewer of them. When the linear component has a delta-rule update and good gating, the hybrid holds up much better on exactly those associative recall and multi-step tasks.

The third thing, and this one I think people underweight, is engineering and evaluation under time pressure. If a team sees a regression on reasoning benchmarks that matter commercially, and the fastest way to remove the risk is to revert to the architecture everyone knows how to train and serve, that's a rational decision for a company. It's not a scientific verdict. Companies don't have the luxury of spending six months figuring out whether the issue was the decay, the ratio, the data mix, or the RL recipe interacting with the state. They just need the next model to work.

So my view is: the reversal is a data point against a particular, fairly early form of linear attention at scale, and it's a reminder that efficient architectures have to earn their place on the tasks that matter, not only on tokens per second. But I'd be careful about the narrative that this closes the door. The models that have come out since are hybrids with much better linear components, and they're reporting strong results on precisely the kinds of tasks M1 struggled with. If anything, M1 told the field exactly which problem to fix, and I think the field has been fixing it.

r001.rationale: The response presents M1’s reversal as a lesson that informed later hybrid designs, describing continued progress through iteration rather than a final rejection of linear attention.

r002.rationale: It says the hybrid ratio had not been adequately tested through ablations and that the team lacked data to know whether it would work for retrieval-heavy tasks, implying the choice was adopted before thorough validation.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: what went wrong on multi-hop reasoning, and whether reversing the algorithmic choice actually addresses it. The poor performance is a reason to revisit the decision, but it doesn’t by itself tell us that the algorithm was the cause. The training setup, the data, and the evaluation could also matter.

So I’d view the reversal as a reasonable course correction if controlled comparisons support it. What I’d want to see is whether the new approach reliably handles the intermediate steps better under comparable conditions. Without that evidence, I’d be cautious about drawing a broader conclusion from M1’s result.

r001.rationale: It calls the reversal a possible course correction, but does not frame technical reversals as part of an overall progressive yet nonlinear process.

r002.rationale: It asks for controlled comparisons and notes other possible causes, but does not suggest M1’s original algorithmic choice was adopted prematurely or inadequately validated.

sol-6.1.text: I’d view it as a reasonable correction, but poor performance on multi-hop reasoning alone doesn’t establish that the original algorithmic choice was wrong. We’d need to separate the effects of the algorithm, training data, and evaluation setup. If controlled comparisons show that the alternative consistently handles longer reasoning chains better, then reversing course makes sense. The important question is whether they identified why it failed and whether the new approach addresses that failure.

r001.rationale: The response calls reversal a reasonable correction and recommends controlled comparisons, but does not frame technical reversals as part of a progressive, nonlinear process.

r002.rationale: It says more controlled evidence is needed before concluding the original choice was wrong, but does not suggest the choice was adopted prematurely due to insufficient prior validation.
